speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Kootenay, Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) inquired as to what representations had been made to my department regarding the renting of certain premises in Toronto. In reply, I may say that the government has been approached by those interested in the construction of a new and modern office building in that city, it being suggested that accommodation could be supplied for the Department of Customs and Excise and also for the Taxation branch. The two departments of the government, that is, the Department of Public Works and the Customs department, have been in conference on this subject with the view, if possible, of providing better accommodation for these departments in the city of Toronto.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Will the minister kindly tell us who have approached the government in this matter?
I do not think that would be fair.
Why not?
I do not think their plans are yet matured.

Has the government
given any undertaking or option of any kind?
No.
Has the Canadian National Railways?
I have no knowledge as to that.

Item agreed to.
Higgin's Shore-wharf repairs, $2,300.
Where is Higgin's Shore?

In Prince county. The expenditure is for repairs. It is recommended by the district engineer. The wharf has been very useful as a shelter for a large number of boats engaged in lobster fishing on the eastern coast of Egmont bay, there being no other landing in that vicinity for this traffic. The wharf is in bad condition, no extensive repairs having been made on it for some years, and unless repairs are soon undertaken it will very soon be impassable.

Item agreed to.
Kier's Shore-wharf repairs, $2,000.
Was any money spent on this work last year?

What is the size of the
pier?

It is about 1,030
feet long. The wharf is an old structure whidh was badly damaged in the hurricane of 1923. It serves a rich agricultural district of several thousand people who have no near railway accommodation. It is the only wharf in the vicinity and it is important that it should be kept in good condition for shipping purposes, it is used by the local schooner trade.
In what county is it?
Prince county.

Item agreed to.
New London-harbour improvements, $20,000.

The minister ought to give some explanation of this item; this is too large an amount for an ordinary wharf.
TMr. Meighcn.]

I have a memorandum which I shall read:
The entrance to the harbour from the gulf of St. Lawrence lies between a rocky headline on the west known as Sims Head and the low sand spit to the east, which is from 500 to 1,500 feet in width,
Works for the improvement of the entrance, which is obstructed by a shifting sand bar, were commenced by the department in 1878 and consisted first of constructing a breakwater 1,050 feet in length on the sand beach on the eastern side; this work being chiefly a round timber open face crib filled with brush and stone, which some years later was extended by a square timber head block 150 feet in length. A breakwater 460 feet in length was also built on the western side of the entrance, the inner 400 feet of which consisted of piles, brush and stone, while the outer portion 60 feet in length was a square timber block 40 feet wide and close piles.
These breakwaters were constructed with a view of confining the ebb current and directing it on to the bar outside, as well as to prevent the sea from washing the sand into the channel inside and running parallel with the eastern breakwater.
This structure is at the entrance of the harbour and the purpose is to prevent the silting of sand from the sea into the channel.
Is this the total amount required for the contract?

No, it will take
$32,000 to complete the contract, but $20,000 is as much as we can spend this year.

What protected the
channel previously?

An old cribwork
which this is to replace.
Will this work be done by contract?
Yes, by tender.
Does the minister in every case advertise for public tenders, or does he send out a select list?

We advertise
publicly.

Is that rule followed in
every case? I have information that in the province of Nova Scotia tenders are not always called for but that a few selected persons are asked to tender.
I do not know of anything of that kind; perhaps the hon. member will igive me the information.

The hon. member for
Halifax (Mr. Black) has information to that effect but he is not here at present. However, I will adc him, when he comes, to give it to the minister.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers

If that is the
case I shall be glad to make an explanation, which I am sure will be satisfactory to my hon. friend.
Whom is this vote intended to elect?	[DOT]

It is primarily
for the good of the people of Prince Edward Island.

Which of these people
in particular?
If the hon. member would like to know, the district is in Queens county.

I think the money will
be spent in vain.

What is the real justification for this vote? The minister says that the work is intended to prevent the sand from silting into the channel. But how did the people get along before this wharf was promised them?

This is not a
new work; there was a structure there many years ago, indeed previous to confederation, but it needs to be replaced.
That is all right.

How many boats were
there last year?

There were two
sea-going vessels and seven inland and coasting vessels.

What does the minister
mean by sea-going vessels?

I suppose they
would be vessels going to Cape Breton.

I would call those
coasters.

So that there were nine
vessels in all. About how many will this $20,000 bring-two more?

The work will
make 'it possible for them to continue to use the haribour.
The same nine?

The same nine
[DOT]or other vessels, I do not know; the vessels do not travel on any schedule but simply come and !go as the demands of the district require.

Are there any fishermen
there?
There are fishing vessels, ibut we have no record of any of the smaller boats. What I have given is taken from the returns of the Customs department.

There were only nine
arrivals throughout the year?

That is, arrivals
entered in the customs return, but we have no record of the 'smaller boats.

But those are the only
vessels of any account that call?

Oh no; there are
fishing vessels as well. The harbour is used by the local trade.
There would be no record unless the vessels carried goods that entered the customs?

Those are the
vessels of which we have any record.

But there would be no
record of vessels going to Cape Breton?

I said Cape
Breton, but they might go anywhere else. I want to be clear on that point. The customs returns show so many vessels having entered and cleared; but as I have said so often, there are local vessels coming and going of which no account is taken.

What is
the total amount that has been spent on this wharf up to the present time?
Up to March 31 of this year, $62,093.20.

Item agreed to.
Nine Mile Creek-wharf repairs, $2,450.

This is to repair
a wharf twenty feet by eighteen feet, the damage having been caused by ice pressure, and to reconstruct entirely the outer portion of the wharf. The surrounding country is rich in agricultural products, and contains several hundred persons, a number of whom are employed in fishing, there being two lobster factories located in the district.

Item agreed to.
Souris-breakwater repairs, $36,500.

This is a considerable sum. It is to keep in repair an important pier or breakwater which forms the harbour at Souris, which is an important harbour of refuge. It is used largely by the fish-

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
ing fleets of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, as well as other fishing vessels that go to the banks off there. The engineer reports;
Since the face of the outer block was damaged in the fall of 1915 nothing has been done to make it secure, and although it has withstood all heavy seas and storms up to the present time much better than anticipated, it is now beginning to show signs of weakness and very serious damage is liable to take place at any time unless the stone face is extended along the seaward face and front of this block. The breakwater is a commercial necessity beyond question, for without the protection it affords Souris as a shipping and fishing centre could not survive.
The work is one of some magnitude, the sum of $498,685.33 having been expended on it up to March 31, 1925.
What is the population of Souris?

The town of
Souris has a population of 1,100. The industries consist of fishing, cold! storage plant, lobster factory, saw mill, and planing mill. I should like to emphasize the fact that this harbour is more than a local harbour for Souris. It is the eastern terminus of the Prince Edward Island railway, now operated by the Canadian National, and is largely used by the fishing fleets that ply off the coast of Nova Scotia. . -
Mr. CALDW'ELL: Is the railway to Souris a narrow gauge railway?
Yes.

Has the government
ever considered widening the gauge so that this portion of the Prince Edward Island railway may be afforded more traffic?
I have no personal knowledge of the matter, but I understand it is under consideration.
This is in the constituency of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) ?
Yes.
I understood he was to be taken care of otherwise.

We are taking
care of breakwaters now.
That remark is worthy of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen).
Is it not true?

I know the local conditions here, and I wish to give some information to the committee. This is essentially a harbour of refuge, and is largely used for that purpose. I myself have counted between
IMr. J. H. King.]
sixty and seventy sail of vessels taking refuge there from a storm. That was before the war when the American fishing fleet operated in the gulf of St. Lawrence. Since the war the Americans do not come into the gulf of St. Lawrence to fish. But Souris is a very important fishing place for the Nova Scotia fleet, and I have frequently counted over thirty sail of vessels in Souris harbour during a storm. These vessels, with their equipment, are worth about $20,000 each, representing a probable total value of $900,000 at least. The average crew would number from eighteen to twenty men, so that the total number of all the fishing crews would be about 600 men. There is no harbour that will take care of that fleet on the north side of Prince Edward Island; this is on the south side near East Point. The fishing business could not be successfully operated in the gulf of St. Lawrence without harbours of refuge. Souris is the first harbour that the vessels could make after rounding East Point, and it is essential for the fishing business. As the minister has stated, Souris is the eastern terminus of the Prince Edward Island railway. The steamer plying between Pictou and the Magdalen islands calls there four times a week. There is also communication by auxiliary schooners propelled by steam power. In addition to that there is the ordinary local traffic. We have a fairly large schooner trade with the west and south coast of Newfoundland, and a reasonable traffic of the same kind with Nova Scotia. This breakwater was commenced before confederation. It was taken over at the time of confederation and has been extended until now it is sufficiently large to accommodate the immense fishing fleet that I have described. It is to be maintained for that purpose, and I say again it is hardly in keeping with the dignity of the leader of the opposition to insinuate that the member representing that part of the county had any unworthy object in recommending this work to the department. The district engineer has strongly recommended it. It is a work on Prince Edward Island that is of interprovincial importance; it is just as advantageous to the fishing fleet of Nova Scotia, and perhaps more, than to the fishermen of Prince Edward Island, although I suppose there would be thirty or forty local crews fishing out of that harbour. These are the facts in connection with this work, and I thought it advisable to give them to the committee.
Then why .the insinuation?

There was no insinuation; it was just the opposite. If the hon. member does not intend' to seek re-election of course he could not possibly have an unworthy object. The hon. member's reasoning has just lapsed for the moment, that is all. My purpose was two-fold. First, I was anxious to get the hon. member to his feet because I thought he would know something of the local circumstances, and as he has shown that he does we now understand the situation much better than if he had not risen.
Thank you.

The minister, however,
is sadly lacking, and one never knows just how sadly lacking he is until just a few days afterwards when he begins to hear the facts from the various localities. I get some startling information from time to time after the words of the minister reach the country. My other object was to find out^perhaps it was an unworthy curiosity-if the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) would deny the aspiration, but I notice he was discreetly silent on that point. Therefore I will have to take it for granted that the suggestion was correct. While we on this side of the House regret to lose' him we certainly agree that in party service he has earned the promotion.

My right hon. friend's
imagination is very strong.

I understood the minister
to say that there had been no damage to this breakwater since 1915. Well, I happen to have visited Souris within the last two years, and walked over that breakwater. My observation then was that it was in a very good state of repair, and I am rather surprised io find now an item of this size in the estimates having regard to the appearance of the pier when I saw it. Of course appearances are deceptive; the structure might be undermined. I quite agree with what the hon. member for Kings has said. Souris is a very important harbour on the southeast coast of Prince Edward Island, and it is quite proper to keep the structure up. But I question very much if at this time this very large expenditure is required; it does not so appear to the casual observer.

My hon. friend,
no doubt, would acquire a great deal of information from visiting Souris and walking over the breakwater, but he failed to observe
the damage that has taken place. The district engineer reports that serious damage was done to the breakwater in 1915, and he recommends very strongly that its face be protected from further action by the sea.
I have not very much faith in the report of the district engineers. They will report almost anything ycu want them to report.
If my hon. friend has that opinion of any district engineer, will he give me his name?
I do not know who he is, but I happen to knew that in years gone by a district engineer could be induced to make almost any report.
Belle River for instance.
Yes, that is a case in point -a most outrageous case.

My hon. friend is discussing something he has no right to discuss. That matter is before the Public Accounts committee and there will be an opportunity to discuss it. And Belle River will be ail right when it comes up. I think it is most unfair of my hon. friend to attack the engineering staff in that way. It will not add to the confidence of the people who have faith in these men. If my hon. friend has in mind any particular engineer he should report him to the department and we will investigate.
' Mr. HANSON: I am much obliged for the castigation of the minister but I did give an instance, namely Belle River, where the facts disclosed show that the engineer's report was most exaggerated. He has doubled the population over and above the official statistics.
We will wait for the evidence.
We have had the evidence.

My hon. friend
has had some evidence, and is interpreting it for his own advantage.

The proceedings before the Public
Accounts committee cannot be discussed.

That may be true and. I
bow to the chairman's decision, but the minister asked a question, I answered it. I think that this is surely an important point, and if the minister is bona fide of The belief that this breakwater requires further expenditure, I

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
am satisfied that it should be made, but I am net just satisfied with the bona tides of the demand. This pier is in the same condition as it was after the storm ten years ago, and the matter can very well stand.

That is contrary
to the report of the engineer.

Item agreed to.
St. Peter's Bay-breakwater and beach protection repairs and reconstruction, $2,000.

What is the traffic
through this port?

This appropriation is urgently required to reconstruct and strengthen portions of a very old work which was damaged and partly carried away by a hurricane which swept over the province, October 1, 1923. The work is wholly of a public nature, affording the necessary landing and protection to several lobster factories and a large fleet of fishing boats.
How much was spent of last year's vote?

The expenditure
in 1924-25 was $3,038.65.

What was done for
that? Was it dredging or wharf repairs?

Last year the vote was late, and the work was commenced at a late date and it was impossible to complete all the necessary repairs during 1924-25. Practically all the material required has now been delivered at site, and the beach protection work, 230 feet long, about completed, while sufficient repairs have been made on the balance of work to secure it until next year.

My hon. friend speaks
of beach protection. What form does it take? Is it in the form of rip-rapping with stone.
It is cribwork with stone.	*
How long?
It is 1,450 feet in length.

Speaking of beach
protection, does that mean to keep it from washing away the shore, or what is the object?
It is the entrance, and this vote is to maintain the harbour.

Is it tc' keep the silt
from washing in? Or to keep it from wearing away the shore-line?
fMr. Hanson.]
It is to keep the bank from going into the channel and blocking.

Will the
amount provided this year complete the job?

Yes, that is the
intention.

The minister said there
were a large number of lobster factories there. Will he tell us how many lobster factories there are, the amount of capital invested and the turnover? On visiting in the locality I was not very much impressed with it as a commercial centre.

I have this
report:
There are three lobster factories nearby employing 75 hands during the fishing seasons, while some 50 fishermen depend wholly on the fishing industry as a means of livelihood.
St. Peter's harbour is the only one on an exposed coast for a distance of 30 miles available for vessels with any considerable draft after rounding East point, and is used quite extensively by vessels of this class during the fishing season besides supplying the necessary shelter for many large motor boats freighting and fishing between the different small harbours along the north coast of the island.

Item agreed to.
Summerside-breakwater repairs, $2,000.

The work proposed is the sheathing of the entire sloping face of the outer block, 130 feet long and 20 feet wide on top, with ten-inch hardwood timber. The district engineer states:
The repairs proposed are entirely of a public nature and considered absolutely necessary in order to maintain a valuable work that gives the necessary protection to the shipping trade of the port of Summerside. As the present plank sheathing has been badly damaged, there is great danger of the entire face of the outer block being carried away by running ice, unless the repairs and strengthening proposed are undertaken at a very early date.

Is the pier faced with
hardwood lumber or boiler plate?
Hardwood.

Item agreed to. .
Tignish harbour-repairs to breakwater, $4,500.

How much was spent on
this?
The amount spent was $133,073.

What is the nature of the
repairs this year?

Supply-Harbours and Rivers

My memorandum reads:
To complete work commenced during 1924-25 consisting of repairs to top portion of seaward wall of north breakwater for an average depth of eight feet and length of 250 feet, also to reconstruct top portion of south breakwater 100 feet long to average depth of six feet. Both of these works are twenty feet wide.

Will the minister
explain to us-and possibly I am revealing my ignorance by asking the question-just what these last words mean?"-"Appropriations not required for 1925-26." In view of the fact that the whole vote for Prince Edward Island last year was $29,000, how does it come that the $73,000 was not required? I see such items appearing in many estimates.

It is a statement
put in by the Finance department in making up their yearly estimates. These moneys have been expended and therefore they are not required.
Having been expended?
Yes.
Expended last year.

Where the items are not
mentioned in this year's estimates?
Yes; they are off the slate.

How much was spent in
Tignish the last year and the year before? It seems to me this has become a hardy annual.

The amount
spent last year-$6,036.
And the year before?

I have not that
information, but I notice in the discussion last year $2,700 was mentioned as the expenditure the year before.

I suppose the minister
could ascertain from the deputy that the year before that there were several thousand more.
No, I think not.

What is the principal
reason why there is so much damage to the breakwater every year?

These breakwaters are subject to the elements, and on an exposed coast there is bound to be damage.
If the breakwater is decaying or out of repair, the damage is greater. Work of this kind requires constant care if it is to be kept in a proper state of repair.

I can understand that
along the Northumberland strait where there is so much ice, but on the east side of the island, is the water frozen up every year?
, It is right on the gulf of St. Lawrence. It is exposed.
Is there ice damage on that side?

I would think
so.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers-New Brunswick-Beaver harbour -wharf repairs, $3,000.
Does the department own this wharf? When was it built and what is the condition of the wharf now?

The wharf was
built in 1909 by the Department of Public Works; it is owned by the government.

Is any revenue derived
from these public wharves?
There would not be from this wharf.

What is the condition of
the structure now?

The engineer
reports that sea worms have destroyed the lower portion of the piles in the section of the work near low water level. Close piling will strengthen the work and, in addition, from a sheltered area back of the pier heads where boats can lie in safety during easterly and southerly storms. The wharf is used by Connors Brothers in landing freight and passengers twice a week and it is used extensively by the fishermen.

Item agreed to.
Black's harbour-reconstruction of wharf approach,

This is a good deal of
money for a wharf approach at Black's harbour. Has a survey been made, and what is the nature of the approach?

The engineer reports that the work has been damaged by ice and it is necessary to construct a block and span approach to the pier head of the wharf, 128 feet long and sixteen feet wide, made up of one shore block forty feet long, two blocks each twenty feet long and three spans each sixteen feet in length.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers

Will $2,000 complete
that structure? It seems quite an extensive structure for that amount. Wihat is the height of the pier?

I have not the
height of the pier.

Will the substructure
of the pier be eribwork and stone?
Yes.

What is the traffic at
Black's harbour?.

All export and
import at Black's harbour are made by water, the nearest rail point being nine miles distant. The steamer Connors Bros, carries freight and passengers to this place for St. John and St. Andrews, and the public wharf is used extensively by other power boats. Black's harbour is the location of the extensive packing plant of Connors Brothers, Ltd. and has a population during the greater part of the year of 500. The annual pack is estimated at $500,000.

Connors Brothers have
their own pier?
Yes.

This wharf is for the
convenience of the fishermen and the public?
Yes.

The steamboat is owned
by the same concern. I understand she uses their own private pier.
They would land at our pier.
Is the minister sure about that? I think he is wrong.

The engineer
states that.
I presume they use this pier -for the general traffic and their own pier for their own private work.
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Burn's (Belle Isle bay)-wharf improvements, $4,500.
Where is this point?
In the county of Royal. At the head of Long reach on the St. John river, I think.
Would it be in Kings or in Queens county-because there is no . "county" of Royal?
Kings.

Item agreed to.

Burnt Church-wharf repairs, $2,500.
This is to put creosoted sheeting on the pierhead, replacing the present wornout covering and cap with concrete.
Will this vote complete the work?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Campbellton-repairs to market wharf and to deep water wharf, $1,800.
What is the nature of this?

The work will consist of replacing the stringers which support the rails across the outer span, continuing filling of the western extension, making minor repairs to deep water wharf and resurfacing the entire surface of the market wharf with broken rock and gravel. This will provide a serviceable covering for several years.
Is this used for shipments of lumber as well as fish?
Largely lumber and fish.

I think there must be something wrong with that information, because lumber from Campbellton is either lightered out from wharves owned by the lumbermen or loaded over private wharves. I do not think they ship the lumber over this wharf. I think it is used for the steamboat service.
: Mr. KING (Kootenay): There are many shipments over this deep water wharf, which is in continual use by steamers and sailing vessels. It is a divisional point on the Canadian National Railways. It is an important point, as I think my hon. friend will agree.

Campbellton and Bathurst are to-day the largest shipping ports of lumber in New Brunswick. There is no doubt that Campbellton as regards shipments of lumber is away ahead even of the port of St. John. This small item is neces-
4 p.m. sary to improve the accommodation.
In addition to lumber we are shipping fish to a certain extent, but not a large quantity, by rail and water. We certainly need this accommodation because we have in the harbour at the present time steamers from across the ocean trying to load up a large quantity of lumber which has been in the yards of the lumbermen throughout the winter. This wharf, I am informed, is necessary for the approach of cars and other means

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
of transportation such as smalLbottom boats that come in between the two wharves, the market wharf and the deep water wharf. The engineer was sent there at the request of the citizens of Campbellton for the purpose of having the facilities improved for the transportation of our products.
Mr. HANSCffc: Do tramp steamers loading lumber at Campbellton use this wharf, or do they anchor in the stream and have the lumber lightered out to them?
I know steamers load their cargoes 'at the wharf. I have seen them do so in previous years.

Item agreed to.
Cape Bald-breakwater repairs, $5,000.

Mr. Chairman, I imagine the name ought to be changed. I do not think the place can be regarded as any longer "bald" after the votes of the last three years. I find that a total of 114,700 has been voted, if not expended. How much has been spent in the last three years on this particular breakwater, and what is the total amount voted to date?

If my bon. friend had an opportunity of visiting the locality he would understand that it is well named cape Bald; it is a bleak, open spot on the coast. In all there has been spent 873,979. Last year we spent $2,544 of the appropriation voted.
How much will be needed to finish this work?
This will complete the repairs we have in hand at the present time.
What has the minister in mind to then occupy the attention of the people down there?

There may be
another storm-they come up pretty regularly.
Has the department any further plans for cape Bald?

Nothing more
than maintenance work.
I hope the minister will be fortified against any further demands.
This is for maintenance work.

Item agreed to.
Cole's point-wharf repairs, $2,700.

Certainly it is all the more reason why we should be more careful of our public expenditure at the present time. If we committed sins- which I do not admit-are they going to copy us on all occasions? That is always their retort: You did pretty much what we 
are doing. But that is no argument. Our expenditures were mainly due to the war. I submit that to-day conditions are bad throughout the country, there is great depression in business and an exodus of our people across the line, and high taxation is largely the cause, and therefore it is all the more important that at this time we cut out every unnecessary expenditure. No matter what was done years ago, it is the duty of the government to act for the present. I submit once more, that it is time in all departments of government to call a halt in expenditure, and that will be our policy if we should get into power at the next election, as I know we will.
Oh, oh.

You need not bother
with the compliment. What is the point of order?

I suggest
to you, Mr. Chairman, that this discussion is entirely out of order, having nothing whatever to do with the vote now being dealt with.

I do not know that
the discussion is altogether out of order, although I agree with the hon. member that it is getting that way; but the question of governmental extravagance, based upon one particular vote, has been generally debated.

I agree with you as to that, Mr. Chairman. The only point I wish to suggest for your further consideration is that we are not now dealing with the question of general policy; the discussion is simply a rehash of the old stoiy of the other party being at fault.

Mr. Chairman. I agree
entirely with my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland), but I think it is a matter for regret that the point was not raised by him sooner. Surely, after this parade of language for campaign purposes, my hon. friend would not expect us to sit here as dumb as oysters and not say a word of correction in reply?
It would be a new experience for the minister.

I agree with the hon. minister, and I think that a straight and proper denial of the remarks, if they can be denied, is admissible. But for the hon. member to go away back into the past history of the party for generations is in my opinion a waste of time. I do not think either of the old parties is worth the time that has been wasted on them in this connection.

I think it would be
reasonably close to the discussion that has been going on to indicate that in the last eight years of the Liberal government's previous regime some $123,000,000 was spent on public works, while in the first four years after 1911 that these hungry gentlemen opposite were in office they spent more than $160,000,000 on public works. And now, when the vote for public works is about as low as any public works vote since they originally took office in 1911, my hon. friends talk about the ladk of economy. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) ought to stick more closely to facts and not undertake to fool the people of his constituency and other constituencies in Canada as he has attempted to do by a parade of figures that are not in accordance with the facts.

One is always delighted,
even aside from whether there is any substance in it or not, to listen to the measured accents of the Minister of Labour. We never know just what the final verdict of an intelligent community is going to be-
We have it in West Hastings.
-until we hear it pronounced.

And we are going to
have it in a few other places too.

We have had a purchased verdict and we are now paying the purchase price. I was anxious a while ago to give the proof but the Minister of Public Works would not let me. This government is not only commencing extravagant expenditures under the conditions of to-day, but- and this is the worst feature-it is launching this year upon large commitments which are only represented in the estimates by relatively small amounts, in order to keep down the total and enable the Minister of Labour to expatiate throughout the country upon the total of this year. But the commitments this year run into fabulous figures. The vote now before us is only one quarter of the total commitment, and the same applies to scores of votes through the list. What is more, this government has abandoned the practice of having the estimates represent, its real com-

mitments for the year. This government ran away from that three years ago and has kept away from it ever since. What about last night's expenditure? Is it in the estimates? Is it a .public work? No, i't is not in the estimates.

Very good; and this

No other government
will be invited to do anything of the kind.

The hon. gentleman's noise would be more appropriate when he is on his feet; it is bad enough ait all times. While I am on my feet I want to give a summary of the knowledge of public affairs on the part of some hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not do this in castigation of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) for I know he dutifully takes his politics from others, and perhaps thalt is the best thing for him to do.
Thank you very much for your courtesy.

But I do it chiefly with reference to the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who is the father of this canard about a large increase in the public debt of this country prior to the war by the late administration. I put before the House on a previous occasion a statement he was reported to have made in Edinonton. I read the report in which he was quoted as saying that we had increased the public debt 46 per cent before the outbreak of the war. I gave the figures then, taken from the public records, and I asked the Minister of the Interior to look it up and see if he made such a statement and if he did not, to rise on the orders of the day and put himself right. We have never heard from him since. The 
public records show-I have them before me -that the debt of Canada, ws increased in the year ending March 31, 1911-that was the last year of the Liberal government-by $3,773,506; that in the year ending March 31, 1912 the debt of Canada, taking in everything, was reduced by a small amount, some $122,591; that in the year ending March 31, 1913 the debt of Canada was reduced $25,647,836. Yes, I still deny them.
I thought he would. It is the function of the hon. gentleman to deny the facts from the public records.

That does not
convey all the truth. These were receipts that were left in the treasury by the other government. Let him go on now and cite the record from that on.

The hon. gentleman talks like a child. Do not let us have such infantile nonsense. If the government had receipts they would put them on the debt. The cash, as anybody knows, at the end of the year is deducted from the national debt for that year. Everybody knows that who has any license to foe out of his cradle. It was in each year of the Liberal government, as it ought to have been, and was in every year under every government. For the year ending March 31, 1914, the year in which we had to provide $15,000,000 for the precious Grand Trunk Pacific railway, the debt of Canada was increased $21,695,000, of which $15,000,000 was to provide for the Grand Trunk, then in decrepitude, left by hon. gentlemen opposite. But aside from the causes, all I want to point out is that the residue of the whole three years shows that instead of an increase right up to the outbreak of the war there was decrease in the public debt of Canada of approximately $4,000,000, a little more.

Will the right
hon. gentleman say that is in accordance with the balance shown in the revenue and expenditure?

No, of course it is not.
Revenue and expenditure is consolidated revenue and consolidated expenditure. This takes in capital, every character of commitment, and gives the net result at the end of the year. That was the result to the outbreak of the war. I have stated this mainly that I

There has been a nasty storm off Escuminac and it only demonstrates the need of a breakwater. But the storm that is taking place here would show a need for a breakwater in other places as well. The hon. member (Mr. Hanson) stated that salmon fishing to-day was being carried on under the same conditions as prevailed in the time of our forefathers, but I am surprised that he should have said such a thing. Salmon fishing on thp Miramichi one hundred and fifty years ago, or on the St. John, where my hon. friend belongs, was a different matter from what it is to-day. And even until within recent times the conditions were altogether different; the men did not go out in such boats as are used nowadays but they used canoes made of pine logs dug out. There was therefore no danger
whatever in connection with the industry at that time. This was the condition that prevailed around Burnt Church and the north shore of the Miramichi river and bay, as well as on the south shore up to Baie du Yin, and around Fox island and Portage island. The men used set nets that were comparatively close to the shores. But the business has materially changed since then; to-day they use boats propelled by motors and they stay out all night. They set a great line of nets three miles off the shore in the outer Miramichi bay and Northumberland straits and they have no protection at all. This matter has been overlooked by the hon. member; I am sure he could not have been aware of it or he would not have made the statement he did.
I should be sorry if the impression got abroad that salmon fishing to-day is the same as it was as carried on by our forefathers.
I was sorry that my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) spoke as he did with reference to the question of annexation or secession. There may be talk of this in his part of the country but I can assure him that in the part of New Brunswick from which I come, and of which I have fairly intimate knowledge, there is very little talk of that kind except on the part of those politicians on the Conservative side who are trying to create this feeling just as they fostered the flag-waving sentiment on a former occasion.

Will the hon. member
say what Conservative politician in New Brunswick has talked secession, and where and when?

They do; but you do
not hear Liberals talking that way either in this House or outside. We have heard it however from the other side. The Liberals today are as loyal to Canada and to British institutions as they were in 1911 when in the interests of this country they wanted to secure trade relations with our friends to the south. At that time the flag was waved all over the country. I do not think it is wise that this talk about secession should get abroad; I do not believe that our people, if they are let alone and not agitated, will think of such a thing. I know that so far as New Brunswick is concerned the people who went to the United States a few years ago are now coming back on a large scale. And the same I have no doubt is true of other parts of Canada. The people will come back in larger numbers if we develop our natural resources in this country, as we are trying to do in the vote which is before parliament this afternoon.

Georgeville-new wharf, $90,000.
But there is not a vessel owned at that place and no person could possibly use the wharf; 
at any rate, there are not more than a dozen fishermen there.

I do net know but the byelection was over, having been won on the promises held out.

Ever since
I came here, I have taken an intense delight in watching the changing expressions on the countenances of hon. members of this House. Whenever one of my friends opposite rises and begins to proclaim the virtues of the Liberal party and the vices of the Conservatives, all other hon. gentlemen on the opposite side smile seraphically and cheer and applaud. But when the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) or any other member on this side gets up, there are black looks and lowering frowns across the way.
That is stretching.

The hon.
member does not frown; his smooth and placid countenance would net be capable of a frown unless a divorce bill was up. I do not wish to discuss the merits or demerits of either party. I simply wish for the sake of the . public to summarize what has happened. In the for y-six years of national life up to the outbreak of the war tihis country under both governments had spent increasing amounts until the enormous total of $451,000,000 had been reached. That means that Canada spent more money than she raised in taxes, to the tune of $800,000 a month or $26,000 a day. No one can claim any great economy for either party at that time, nor am I going to argue that it was a good thing that there should have been particular economy, providing the expenditures were justified; because after all we were a growing nation in need of public works and other things. But since the war, what has happened on both sides? We have spent the following sums:
1919		 $697,000,000
1920		 785,000,000

Today that sum of money would permit the purchase in cash of the entire Canadian Pacific holdings in equipment, rolling stock, and ocean vessels, and still leave enough over to buy all the chartered banks of Canada. It

is true that 57 cents out of every dollar of that money is the result of war itself, and if ever there was a bitter, biting indictment of militarism the results left on a nation of this size by war would demonstrate it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to come back again to this vote of $50,000 for Escu-minac. The only grounds for it that I have heard are two-fold. The first is that it was promised in 1911 and in 1882. The second is that the fishermen of the district need some protection from storms. One hon. member pictured the dangers to which the fishermen are exposed, but another hon. member from the same province stated there has not been one life lost. I do not know which to believe, and that is the position I find myself in. If I can find justification for this item in the saving of life or in the' protection of the people immediately concerned, I am willing to vote for it. I am not willing to vote for it, however, if those interested do not need it; and in any ease expenditures of this kind should be justified1 to a greater degree by the minister who is proposing them.
I should like to ask the minister, arising out of a remark he made that this whole scheme will cost $209,000, just what the government .proposes to do?

That is for the breakwater?
Mr. KING (Kootenay); Yes. We are proposing to construct one section of the breakwater which when completed will give a very considerable amount of protection to the fishing boats. That is as far as we intend going at the present time.

How long will the unit
be that you are going to construct?

It will be about
400 feet long.

I regret very much indeed that a discussion of this nature should have taken place this afternoon on the New Brunswick item, and this, special item in particular. On the eastern and southern portion of the province of New Brunswick we have an exposed coast line with the exception of twelve miles; in a great many cases there is no railway accommodation whatever, and it is very necessary that there should be some facilities provided for water transportation in these localities. I am sure if hon. gentlemen will stop to consider the necessities of the fishermen living along these shores who have to go out on the water at night-time they will say that it was reasonable there should be some protection for them. Nearly every year we have very severe storms in that district; .property is sometimes lost and at times life is lost because of insufficient protection for the fishing boats. I have been in this particular place and realize the situation, although I have no personal interest there. The fishermen go ouit there to fish

and they have no protection in that particular port.
What sort of protection does the minister think will be provided by this vote?

I will come to that later.
This is a very open and exposed coast, and when fishermen are out in the straits or come in with their boats they are sometimes washed up on the shore, and there is no haven of rest to protect them from the sea. I am as anxious for economy as any hon. member in this House, and I can assure hon. members that before the estimates were brought down, instead of asking for large votes, I simply asked, as far as New Brunswick was concerned, for whatever was necessary to protect the fishermen and to provide for their wants.
Does the hon. minister not think that the same facilities for protection which they have had for many years would not have sufficed for a few yeans until we started to reduce our debt?

I say that the fishermen are

Can the minister tell us
how many fishermen are employed in this particular locality?

The minister gave the number, I have not it in mind. I am sure that hon. members from the Maritime provinces, the hon. member for York-Sunbury and the hon. member for Kent, know the conditions down there and realize that the coast of Kent is exposed to the storms in the Northumberland straits. They know that we must have protection. I regret that my hon. friends from the west, for whom I have great esteem, who stood loyally by us in working in the interests of western Canada as well as other parts of Canada, took the stand they did this afternoon, because they have no knowledge of the conditions. These works are necessary to protect the interests of the fishermen on the shores of New Brunswick. These votes are not the result of promises I have made, and I say that in all cases I have urged economy as far as possible in regard to the requirements of the locality, and the estimates brought down are very small indeed. >
The estimates for New Brunswick only amount to about fifty cents a head for every man, woman and child in the province. I do not think my hon. friends realize the necessity for taking care of the situation in the province of New Brunswick as they should. We realize that for the last year or two conditions have not been good in these provinces. A number of our people are leaving there because the fishermen are not protected. People have left the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and gone to the United States for the reason I have stated. A great many of our men are engaged in this valuable industry, and I do hope that my hon. friend will think better of the amendment he has moved and allow this motion to pass.

As I view it, this amendment is a demand upon the hon. members of this House for a declaration for or against national economy. Many of us do not know much about the locality or about the protection of the fishermen; but in the discussion which we have listened to this afternoon hon. members on the government side have said, "Well, a number of years ago, before the wai and during the war, you spent so much and we spent so much, and therefore you should keep your mouths shut. You have nothing to say." I know, and every hon. member here must know, that from one end of Canada to the other the real issue in the public mind is, will the governments federally, provinciallv and municipally stop their extravagance and live within their revenue? This amendment is calling upon hon. members to act in their capacity as representatives of the people in a manner which will show whether they will be consistent to their declarations at election time or not. We have a debt of $2,400,000,000. As I mentioned last evening, we have greatly increasing taxation, business more or less paralyzed and people leaving the coun-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item under discussion is No. 147, harbours and rivers, New Brunswick, Escuminac harbour improvements, $50,000.

Before six o'clock the discussion had got to a point somewhat wide of the mark, and I am not sure that the interests of the people whom we are trying to assist were all under consideration. This project is not a new one; it has'been before the department for some time, having been recommended by responsible members of parliament. As has been pointed out, Mr. Loggie, a former representative of the district, as well as Hon. Mr. Hazen, at one time Minister cf Marine, both advised it. It is all very well to say that these people got along without this accommodation for many years and that there is no need of it at the present time. I do not agree with that, and it is not the attitude of the public tc-day. It has been brought to the attention of this House during this session that in the Maritime provinces, where the government had failed to provide the necessary improvements or to enlarge present facilities, many of the people had found it necessary to go away. That sort of thing is not in the interests of the country. The people of the Maritime provinces along the coast are engaged very extensively in fishing, which is an important and profitable industry. It is a great source of wealth to them, and to strike out practically the whole of this vote, as is now recommended, would work a very great injury to the business by which they gain their livelihood. The amount may seem large but to-day I explained that there were something like 130 boats using the harbour besides about 50 dories; and that indicates what a considerable number of men are engaged in the business of fishing. If the committee will look over the votes that we have placed in the estimates this year they will find that almost in every case these items are for repairs or improvements; in very few instances have new items been inserted. As a matter of fact, as I stated this afternoon, the total estimates this year for the department are $1,700,000 less than they were last year. I would ask the hon. member (Mr. Kellner) to be good enough to reconsider his motion to reduce the vote. I am satisfied that the
expenditure is warranted, and if the work contemplated is not carried out it will mean a very serious hardship to the people in that locality. I am sure the hon. member must realize that the proposed reduction would be unsound policy; we must maintain our great public works in Canada to-day. If there is a community that can be helped by a reasonable expenditure such expenditure ought to be made. For these reasons I would ask the hon. member to withdraw the motion.

The minister suggests
looking over the estimates; I presume that is an invitation to consider any of the estimates in his department. I wculd call his attention particularly to the expenditures in the western provinces. Take Manitoba; the vote there this year is $27,300 as compared with $68,970 for last year. Neither Saskatchewan nor Alberta had a sufficient expenditure to warrant its being put in a separate column and so the two are bunched together; and the combined expenditure in these two provinces this year is $24,800 as against $46,895 last year. In all the estimates of (the minister's department this is the only example we have of economy, and it affects the prairie provinces. In the discussion of these estimates to-day, member after member has got up and roundly criticized the government for not abstaining from making new expenditures. I think the motion to reduce the vote will test the sincerity of those who advocate economy. As to any hardship that would be suffered by the people concerned, I rather think that perhaps it might be a greater hardship to give them too many facilities. You must provide a market or they will not be justified in increasing their production. From the information I have regarding the district down there, there is either no market or not enough for the fish caught now.

Where did the hon.
member get that, information? I come from the locality and I can assure him that every fish caught there can be sold either in the United States or in upper Canada.

That remark seems to be enthusiastically received, but it is possible that the price is not high enough to make it worth while for the fishermen to catch more. At any rate I know that the farmers of western Canada increased the price of wheat this year by something like a dollar a bushel by the very simple expedient of growing less, and I doubt whether this will not apply to the fishermen of the Maritime provinces. Now, I have no desire to reduce this expenditure, but in view of the statements that have been made in the
Supply'-Harbours and Rivers

House this afternoon I think that the motion is advisable; as I have said, it will test the sincerity of those who are opposing the vote. We shall see whether they will vote against an item which they previously apposed and declared should not be in the estimates.

I would ask tihe hon. member to withdraw the motion to strike out nearly the whole of the vote. We have in Canada both an east and a west. We have our problems in the Maritime provinces, which are very serious indeed, just as the western people in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have their grave problems. But we cannot ever build up a united 'Canada if we are not going to assist each other. I do not desire to see any division between east and west; but-

We realized this very
thing when the Hudson Bay railway debate was in progress.

And we realized it last
night too. I was in this House several years ago when we inaugurated a National Transcontinental railway scheme. Sir Wilfrid Laurier dreamed of a united Canada and desired that Canadian grain for export should go through Canadian ports. We spent a tremendous amount of money to bring the grain of the west to Quebec, and if Sir Wilfrid Laurier had lived after building the railway he would have spent a considerable sum no doubt in improving the facilities at Quebec. Because if we did not have facilities there what would be the use of the railway? What was the use of the bottle if the neck was not big enough for the trade to get out? Sir Wilfrid Laurier's government was defeated and another party came into power that had no love for the National Transcontinental. They showed it by their actions, and so very little was done to improve the facilities at Quebec during the years that the present opposition were in power in this country.

Is the hon. member not
aware that nearly all the great expenditures in providing facilities at the port of Quebec were made by the harbour commission under the presidency of Senator Lesperance, and the money was supplied by the Conservative party in 1911?

I think, Mr. Chairman, that the money expended by the harbour commission under the supervision of Senator Lesperance did not provide facilities for transporting more than five or six million bushels 
out of a total of two or three hundred million bushels of grain.

This discussion has
no reference to the construction of a breakwater in New Brunswick.

I quite appreciate that but
what I am contending is this:	While we in
the Maritime provinces had not any direct interest in Quebec nor in the shipment of western wheat, through that port when the National Transcontinental was put through, yet hundreds of millions of dollars were spent upon that road and not a single yard of the line was built in the province of Nova Scotia from which I come. But when Sir Wilfrid Laurier appealed to the people of Canada the electors of Nova Scotia sent back to this House a solid group of eighteen to support him in building this great road from the west.
Perhaps the hon. member will tell us what advantage accrued to the west from the building of that road?

There has been some
advantage to the west, but the reason the advantages were not as great as Sir Wilfrid Laurier thought they would be was because the road was to a large extent destroyed by its enemies. The gradients and the curvatures of that line were increased.
Order.

I am only answering a
question that was put to me.

speechtext:
You are wandering
from the point.

I ask the hon. member,
in all honesty, does he believe that?

Of course I believe it. If I did not believe it I would not make the statement. But, Mr. Chairman, the vote before the House is for a breakwater for the benefit of the fishermen on the coast of New Brunswick. All that is asked for here is a vote of $50,000. We are told by the member for the county that if this breakwater is built it will probably mean that there will be a million dollars worth of fish caught and brought into Canada. What is the hope of Canada? The hope of Canada lies in found money, whether we find it in the sea, in the soil, in the mine, or in the forest. That is the great hope of our country, and that is why we do not wish to travel the via dolorosa we hear talked about so much

Supply-Harbours and. Rivers
in the far corner of the House. We have faith in the future of Canada because we know the natural resources are here from which we can secure the riches that will ensure the prosperity of this country in the future. We have in eastern Canada great fisheries. Instead of having a production of eight or ten million dollars from the sea we should have a production of fifty or sixty million dollars from that source-found money for Canada. If fishermen go out and catch a million dollars worth of fish, and bring those fish to shore and sell them in a foreign market it means a million dollars added to the wealth of Canada. These fishermen are men who deserve our sincere sympathy. If my hon. friends who live on the golden prairie plains knew exactly what hardships these men suffer I think they would have more sympathy with them than they have to-night. I expect that in a few days-at any rate I hope before this session closes-there will be a proposition to provide railway facilities to open up the great Peace river country. It does not interest me directly, I come from away down by the sea where the fishermen live, but I will support the proposition because it means a better and a bigger Canada. I would ask hon. gentlemen to-night to take the same view that I take in reference to the Peace river, and not vote to reduce this amount for the building of what, after all, is a necessity to the fishermen who certainly earn their living by the sweat of their brow.
This afternoon we heard a very eloquent and rapid-fire speech from the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). According to him we may as well put up the shutters

I never suggested any

I never suggested any
such thing.

We are now discussing a vote included in the estimates which amounts to $228,300 for a whole province, and if my hon. friend is honest in this matter he will accept my challenge. I find here on page 31 of the estimates this item: "Port Arthur and Fort William harbour improvements, $120,000." Last year there was a vote for the same purpose of $550,000 or more than twice as much as the whole vote for the province of New Brunswick. As I have already said the 237
estimate! for these improvements amounts this year to $120,000. I challenge the hon. gentleman when we come to that vote to move to reduce it. That will show his sincerity.

The government is quite
free to reduce it as far as I am concerned. I accept my hon. friend's challenge. Let the government go ahead and reduce it.

It is your place to move
the reduction.

One would imagine to hear
the hon. member for Cumberland that the only place in Canada where any fishing is done is on the Atlantic coast. It may surprise him to know that there is a greater coast line in the constituency which I represent than in any constituency in the Maritime provinces. I venture this further statement-that there is more fish produced in my constituency than in any constituency in the Maritime provinces.
Oh, oh.
More fish produced?
Yes, more fish produced.
We produced last year between eight and ten million dollars' worth.

I say there is more fish
produced in my constituency than any constituency in the Maritime provinces. Yet in the entire history of that constituency only $9,700 has been spent on public wharves. There are some thirty or forty fishing depots in that constituency, and a number of small towns whose people live almost entirely by fishing, and they are not coming to this House and asking for votes of $50,000 or $100,000 to carry on their fishing. They build their own little wharves where they can dock their fishing boats, and so on. They are carrying on their business without government aid and producing fish by the hundreds of car loads. What is the matter with the Maritime provinces? I will tell you what the trouble is. It is traditional, it is hereditary with you people down there. Every man who is farming or fishing along the coast line imagines he should have a wharf at his back door. There is no question about that.
Do not insult us, please.

I must protest against this
vote. I shall not support it.

Just before the House rose at six o'clock the right hon. leader of the opposition challenged statements of

mine regarding the increase in expenditures during the years 1911, 1912 and 1913. I have not had very much time to look the matter up, but referring to the Public Accounts at page 47 I find that the increase in 1912 was $11,000,000; in 1913 it was $14,000,000; and in 1914 it was $15,000,000.
What is that?

That has never been controverted, and it can be shown in an itemized way that those figures are correct.

Perhaps it would be
somewhat irrelevant to endeavour to answer where there was nothing to answer, but the hon. gentleman got into a subject altogether apart from that which formed the matter of controversy before dinner. In regard to the remarks
of my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) where he threw out a challenge with reference to the expenditure in Fort William and Port Arthur, I want to point out in the first place that it is rather an extraordinary thing to compare a little fishing village, where there are only 1,500 people in the entire neighbourhood and probably half of them fishermen, with a port such as we find at the head of the lakes, where they handle seven-eighths or perhaps nine-tenths of all the grain grown in the prairie provinces. Probably nine-tenths of the grain grown in the prairie provinces goes through the elevators at the head of the lakes. No expenditure made at the head of the lakes has ever been made for the people at the head of the lakes. The port up there is just as much a national port as Montreal or Quebec in Canada or Duluth, Chicago or New York in the United States; so that there is no comparison. I wish to say this-and I put it on Hansard the other night and showed my sincerity by my remark on that occasion-that I am sincere in believing that we should cut down unnecessary taxation and expenditure. I am perfectly willing that Fort William and Port Arthur should receive the same treatment as the other ports of the Dominion, and that we should cut out

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
all unnecessary expenditure from one end of Canada to the other. I repeat that I think there has already 'been sufficient money spent at the head of the lakes to satisfy them for some time. I think we have enough harbour development there now for all the purposes for which that harbour has been developed. There has been a large amount of money spent in that district, but the harbour there has been developed for the handling of grain. I am perfectly agreeable that they should receive the same treatment up there as is accorded to other places, and I will submit to the House after the next election-I do not care who is in power, although I believe it will be the Conservatives [DOT]-that it is high time that all expenditure, whether at 'Halifax, Fort William, Port Arthur, Vancouver, or any other place, shall be curtailed in the interest of economy in this country.

While Escuminac may not be a very important p'ace, it is on a coast where there are millions of fish that can be caught if facilities are provided, and if they are caught and sold it adds to the wealth of the country. I think if the hon. member wishes to be consistent, when we come to the vote for Fort William, he will move that the item of $120,000 be reduced by at least $100,000.
I desire to place on Hansard a statement showing what has been spent at the head of the lakes, which we in the Maritime provinces have helped to pay. The expenditure by the government of this country at Fort William and Port Arthur up to March 31, 1925, has amounted to $14,627,750, and it has been made to provide for transporting the grain from the west.

If I may be permitted to bring the discussion back to Escuminac, I wish to say that I could easily accept the challenge of the hon. member to vote against any public works in my own constituency because that constituency is blessed1 this year with an expenditure of $1,800, while it has the largest coast line of almost any county in the Maritime provinces.
The hon. member boasted last year that he got more than anybody else.

Last year when the estimates of the Minister of Public Works were being considered on the 26th May and 18th July, I asked the minister for a small vote to accommodate 76 fishing boats, 7 canning factories, in a large territory, and 22,7 h
yet the minister said that owing to the necessity for practical economy the department or the government could not see their way clear to make the expenditure. He promised, however, to take the matter into consideration and give it serious thought for this year. The estimates for this year show nothing for that important fishing settlement. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to oppose this vote, because after all I think the members of this committee have taken it too seriously all afternoon. I for one do not believe that the expenditure will be made. I think the minister would be well advised if he would consider the advisability of having surveys made of the neighbouring fishing village of Baie Ste-Anne where to my mind, from the report which I have received, there would be better accommodation and better protection for the fishermen of that section. at a fyace called Blind River which was discussed the other day?

out the paper?

The St. Maurice
Pulp and Paper Company.

it is for the general use.

I did not say that.

The shed and the storage will be a convenience which the people will pay for.

I do not know.

Well, I think my guess was about right. Is it the practice to build sheds for concerns? I know it is the practice to keep up their wharves at select places, but I did not know that we built sheds too.

I think it is better for the department, to build the shed at that point rather than that the company should *build their own shed for their own purposes. This shed will be used by the public generally as well as by the company.

But the department could have a policy whereby sheds on public wharves would be open to the public at the usual fee and in that way the whole country would be relieved of a large expenditure, while the man that built the shed would be paid.
I think this plan will work beter.

I should like to know anything else of the minister's .that has worked out IMr. Meighen.]
better than this will. If the minister will look over the revenue he has derived from these expenditures he will find that he can put them all in the hollow of his hand.
Mr. OR.DRAIi: I desire again to protest as I did the other day in connection with a similar vote for a shed at a place called Blind River. The principle is a bad one and I trust the minister will see that his colleague of the .Marine department (Mr. Cardin) will collect at least sufficient revenue from this shed to payall expenses in connection with it including depreciation and interest on the investment.
I think that will be done.

Perhaps I could throw a little light on this matter; I know something about wharves and sheds. The government, for instance, builds a wharf at some point in Nova Scotia, we will say. A subsidized steamer calls there and lands three or four boxes of sugar besides cement and other articles, late at night. What is to become of those things? Are they to lie on the wharf all night long even though there may be a rain storm? There must be some place in which to store them. Hon. members might say that the public should put up a building; but where would they put it-on government property? So far as I know anything about sheds in Nova Scotia, they are usually very small buildings; there is a small waiting room in the front and a store room at the back. Those that I have seen would not be bigger than forty by twenty feet; in fact, that would be a large one. People waiting on the wharf for a boat during a storm would be in a very bad way if they had nowhere to wait. I think that the present vote will serve a real need. Of course, I do not suggest that the government should enter on any tremendous expenditure, building warehouses for the benefit of the general public; but I do believe that there is a need in this regard, il have been in a great many places where I was glad to have some place in which to shelter while I was-waiting for a boat during a storm. I might explain it in this way: The necessity has come to be real. I do not think that where perishable goods are landing they should be left out on a wharf over night unsheltered. What would the hon. member suggest in a case of that kind?

I would suggest that the district that benefits from the shed, o* the transportation company that is deriving revenue from the carriage of passengers and.

freight should provide the shed. I quite appreciate, I think, the position that my hon. friend and his constituency are in, and probably a good many other constituencies where these sheds are necessary. But I do submit, in all honesty and sincerity, that it is not a sound principle that the general taxpayers of Canada should be taxed to provide facilities for any traffic of this character. The question involved is one of principle. For instance, in my own constituency there is a lake that is becoming in a very considerable measure a summer resort. I think I would be just as much justified in coming to this House and asking for a vote of money to build a shed on the wharf on that lake for the convenience of the passengers there, as the hon. member who represents this constituency is in asking for this vote. Still I do not think the principle is sound, and I wish to say that future expenditures of this kind should be carefully scrutinized.

Perhaps I may be allowed a word or twro further by way of explanation. We have in Nova Scotia warehouse companies that build warehouses for the convenience of people that are shipping apples and potatoes, or people that are receiving coal. They never use the government warehouse for purposes of that kind. In most places the government shed is a small structure that serves to shelter people in inclement weather, and allows perishable goods to be stored until whoever wants them can come and get them. I quite agree with my hon. friend. I do not believe this country should be taxed to build private warehouses. But I can see no reason when a steamer lands at a wharf why some kind of shelter should not be given to passengers waiting to board a boat, especially if the vessel is subsidized and running under government auspices.
Mr. STE\ENS: This is a different case. Here we have a large plant established m the locality, and the minister tells us there is now a very large movement of merchandise coal and sulphur inward; pulp and paper, and kraft paper outward-and the tonnage which he mentioned is very extensive. Consequently we are justified in coming to the conclusion that this shed is being built to especially accommodate the tonnage of this plant. I am not complaining about that, but what I do suggest is that where a shed or other accommodation is obviously placed at the public expense for a private concern there ought to be sufficient revenue coming from it to amortize the capital cost and pay a reasonable interest on the carrying charge.

before me that information. I may say, however, the Cap de la Madeleine is a very important place. Will the minister permit
me this question?
